title: Fast and High-Fidelity Motional-State-Preserving Transport in Optical Tweezers
authors: Wen-hao Wang, Jian-gong Hu, Guang-ming Huang, Gao-xiang Li, Cheng Sheng
abstract: Reconfigurable neutral-atom processors require rapid, high-fidelity transport of atoms between optical-tweezer sites. In finite-depth Gaussian traps, fast motion can leave residual motional excitation even when the atom reaches its destination. We develop a basis-parameterized gradient-ascent pulse-engineering (GRAPE) framework for one-dimensional transport of a single $^{87}$Rb atom. A shortcut-to-adiabaticity reference is refined using 17 trajectory parameters, with ten additional parameters providing bounded trap-depth modulation; depth affects both confinement and the inverse construction of the physical trap center. For a $12.6\,μ$m transfer completed in only $30.5\,μ$s, corresponding to approximately $2.75$ periods of the reference trap, the selected joint protocol achieves a ground-state infidelity of $2.41\times10^{-7}$. Because preparing an exactly pure motional ground state is experimentally challenging, we also optimize population-weighted transport for initial distributions with mean vibrational occupations $\nbar\simeq0.16$ and $1.87$, reaching same-state probabilities of about $0.99993$ and $0.9934$. Trap-depth fluctuations can further degrade transport fidelity. Robust optimization under a measurement-informed depth-noise model improves the mean error, worst sampled error, and fidelity dispersion for the specified noise realizations. Coordinated control of tweezer position and confinement thus offers a route to rapid transport with low residual excitation for flexible atom rearrangement and dynamic connectivity in neutral-atom processors.
summary: This paper presents a sophisticated quantum control protocol using GRAPE to guide neutral atoms rapidly between optical tweezer sites. By jointly optimizing both the tweezer's position and its confinement depth, the authors achieved extremely low motional excitation during transport. This demonstrates a key technological step toward building flexible and high-fidelity quantum processors based on trapped atoms.
main_problem: The core challenge is achieving rapid, high-fidelity transport of neutral atoms between optical-tweezer sites while minimizing residual motional excitation.
main_result: The developed joint control protocol achieved a ground-state infidelity of $2.41 	imes 10^{-7}$ for a $12.6 \mu	ext{m}$ transfer in $30.5 \mu	ext{s}$, demonstrating robust, low-excitation transport.
method: The authors employed a basis-parameterized Gradient-Ascent Pulse Engineering (GRAPE) framework, optimizing control over both tweezer position and confinement depth simultaneously.
model_or_system: The system involves a single $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atom confined in a time-dependent Gaussian potential created by optical tweezers. The dynamics are governed by a time-dependent Gaussian Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Ground-state infidelity, population-weighted same-state transport probabilities, mean error, and worst sampled error under noise.
important_parameters: Transfer distance ($12.6 \mu	ext{m}$), transfer time ($30.5 \mu	ext{s}$), and the number of control parameters (up to 27).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a measurement-informed depth-noise model for robustness testing, and the local harmonic approximation is used for auxiliary references.

paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for fast transport, develops the basis-parameterized GRAPE framework incorporating depth modulation, optimizes for ground-state and population-weighted fidelity, and concludes by testing the robustness of the protocol against depth noise.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of quantum state preservation during dynamic manipulation, which is crucial for scaling up neutral-atom quantum processors and quantum simulation platforms.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Single-atom transport and control objective. A Gaussian optical tweezer carries the atom from site A to site B with center x0(t) and depth U(t). The initial state is either the motional ground state or an incoherent mixture with populations pn. A common waveform is used to preserve the occupied motional-state labels. Here T denotes tf. The potential-energy zero and illustrative depth excursion are schematic, whereas Eq. (1) uses zero potential at infinity and the numerical depth modulation is bounded by 5%.

FIG. 2. Ground-state transport over L = 12.6 µm. (a)–(e) use tf = 28.5 µs: (a) physical trap centers for STA, trajectory- only, and joint protocols, with the auxiliary qc(t); (b) optimized center corrections relative to STA; (c) joint depth U(t)/U0; (d) terminal populations Pn for the displayed vibrational states; (e) infidelity across accepted iterations of the trajectory-only, depth-coupled, and full-joint stages; vertical guides mark the stage boundaries. (f) Terminal infidelities for separately optimized 30.5- and 28.5 µs tasks after refined repropagation. The STA bars are shown at unity scale.

FIG. 3. Ground-state joint control under varied transport conditions. (a) Distance scan at tf = 30.5 µs. (b) Duration scan at L = 12.6 µm. Each marker denotes a separately opti- mized waveform followed by independent refined propagation. Neighboring markers are discrete tasks rather than a contin- uous fidelity frontier.

FIG. 4. Controls and state-resolved transport for two ini- tial motional distributions. (a) Low-lying Gaussian-spectrum populations. (b) Physical center waveforms; the inset shows their differences from the ground-state control. (c) Relative depth waveforms. (d) Same-state probabilities Fn for reuse of the ground-state control and for separately optimized en- semble controls. Population-weighted fidelities are reported in the text; initial-state truncation checks are given in Ap- pendix A. For the shared ground-state waveform, overlapping state labels have the same Fn; only their statistical weights differ.
